The results reveal an antiferromagnetic ordering at $T_N \approx$ (to be determined experimentally) and strongly anisotropic magnetic behavior consistent with a dominant crystal electric field (CEF) contribution. Analysis of the thermodynamic data within a CEF model indicates that the Ce$^{3+}$ $J = 5/2$ multiplet splits into three Kramers doublets with an unusually small energy separation between the ground and first excited states, giving rise to an effective quasi-quartet ground state. This quasi-quartet nature manifests itself in the enhanced Sommerfeld coefficient, reduced ordered moment, and deviations from conventional single-doublet CEF behavior, highlighting the importance of low-lying CEF levels in governing the correlated electron phenomena in CeAg$_2$Ge$_2$.
label: llm

text: We study the properties of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet with spatiallyanisotropic nearest-neighbour exchange couplings on the kagome net, i.e. withcoupling J in one lattice direction and couplings J' along the other twodirections. For J/J' > 1, this model is believed to describe the magneticproperties of the mineral volborthite. In the classical limit, it exhibits twokinds of ground states: a ferrimagnetic state for J/J' < 1/2 and a largemanifold of canted spin states for J/J' > 1/2. To include quantum effectsself-consistently, we investigate the Sp(N) symmetric generalisation of theoriginal SU(2) symmetric model in the large-N limit. In addition to thedependence on the anisotropy, the Sp(N) symmetric model depends on a parameterkappa that measures the importance of quantum effects. Our numericalcalculations reveal that in the kappa-J/J' plane, the system shows a rich phasediagram containing a ferrimagnetic phase, an incommensurate phase, and adecoupled chain phase, the latter two with short- and long-range order. Wecorroborate these results by showing that the boundaries between the variousphases and several other features of the Sp(N) phase diagram can be determinedby analytical calculations. Finally, the application of a block-spinperturbation expansion to the trimerised version of the original spin-1/2 modelleads us to suggest that in the limit of strong anisotropy, J/J' >> 1, theground state of the original model is a collinearly ordered antiferromagnet,which is separated from the incommensurate state by a quantum phase transition.
label: human

text: We investigate the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet with anisotropic exchange couplings on the Kagome lattice as a minimal model for the magnetic properties of the mineral volborthite, Cu₃V₂O₇(OH)₂·2H₂O. Using a combination of exact diagonalization, series expansion, and variational approaches, we map out the ground-state phase diagram as a function of the exchange anisotropy. We identify several competing ground states, including quantum spin-liquid–like regimes, short-range ordered phases, and magnetically ordered states stabilized by anisotropy. The static and dynamic spin structure factors are computed and compared to neutron scattering data, revealing characteristic signatures of short-range correlations and diffuse scattering consistent with experimental observations. We further calculate the uniform magnetic susceptibility and heat capacity, demonstrating that anisotropic exchange substantially improves agreement with available thermodynamic measurements on volborthite relative to the isotropic Kagome model. Our results highlight the role of exchange anisotropy in lifting classical degeneracies, selecting particular quantum ground states, and shaping the low-energy excitation spectrum. We show that moderate anisotropy can account for the absence of conventional long-range magnetic order down to low temperatures in volborthite while allowing for strong short-range correlations. The theoretical predictions for field-dependent magnetization and low-temperature specific heat suggest experimental tests that can discriminate between different proposed microscopic parameter sets.
label: llm

text: Six of the eight double neutron stars known in the Galactic disk have loworbital eccentricities (< 0.27) indicating that their second-born neutron starsreceived only very small velocity kicks at birth. This is similar to the caseof the B-emission X-ray binaries, where a sizable fraction of the neutron starsreceived hardly any velocity kick at birth (Pfahl et al. 2002). The masses ofthe second-born neutron stars in five of the six low-eccentricity doubleneutron stars are remarkably low (between 1.18 and 1.30 Msun). It is arguedthat these low-mass, low-kick neutron stars were formed by the electron-capturecollapse of the degenerate O-Ne-Mg cores of helium stars less massive thanabout 3.5 Msun, whereas the higher-mass, higher kick-velocity neutron starswere formed by the collapses of the iron cores of higher initial mass. Theabsence of low-velocity single young radio pulsars (Hobbs et al. 2005) isconsistent with the model proposed by Podsiadlowski et al. (2004), in which theelectron-capture collapse of degenerate O-Ne-Mg cores can only occur in binarysystems, and not in single stars.
label: human

text: Double neutron star systems provide a unique laboratory for probing the physics of neutron-star formation and subsequent binary evolution. In this work we present a comprehensive analysis of measured masses, orbital parameters, spin periods, and space velocities of known double neutron star binaries in the Galaxy. We identify two distinct subpopulations that differ systematically in their orbital eccentricities, systemic velocities, and inferred natal kick velocities. The first group shows high eccentricities and large peculiar velocities, consistent with formation via canonical iron core-collapse supernovae with substantial mass ejection and strong natal kicks. The second group exhibits low eccentricities, modest systemic velocities, and relatively small inferred kicks, favoring an origin in ultra-stripped or electron-capture supernovae with reduced mass loss. We demonstrate that these two channels can be naturally reproduced in binary population synthesis models that track detailed mass transfer and pre-supernova stripping. The coexistence of these formation channels has important implications for the Galactic double neutron star merger rate.
label: llm

text: We propose and study a model with glassy behavior. The state space of themodel is given by all triangulations of a sphere with $n$ nodes, half of whichare red and half are blue. Red nodes want to have 5 neighbors while blue oneswant 7. Energies of nodes with different numbers of neighbors are supposed tobe positive. The dynamics is that of flipping the diagonal of two adjacenttriangles, with a temperature dependent probability. We show that this systemhas an approach to a steady state which is exponentially slow, and show thatthe stationary state is unordered. We also study the local energy landscape andshow that it has the hierarchical structure known from spin glasses. Finally,we show that the evolution can be described as that of a rarefied gas withspontaneous generation of particles and annihilating collisions.
label: human

text: A topological glass is proposed as a novel disordered phase characterized by topological constraints rather than conventional chemical or positional disorder. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework in which glassy behavior emerges from frustration between competing topological sectors in an otherwise ordered system. Using a combination of lattice models and continuum field theories, we demonstrate that slow dynamics and aging arise from the proliferation of topologically protected defects that cannot be removed by local moves. We show that the resulting energy landscape is hierarchically organized by topological invariants, leading to an extensive multiplicity of metastable states. Numerical simulations reveal dynamical arrest and nontrivial relaxation spectra that are distinct from those of structural and spin glasses but share key phenomenological signatures such as stretched-exponential relaxation.
label: llm

text: Clear evidence for symplectic symmetry in low-lying states of $^{12}$C and$^{16}$O is reported. Eigenstates of $^{12}$C and $^{16}$O, determined withinthe framework of the no-core shell model using the JISP16 $NN$ realisticinteraction, typically project at the 85-90% level onto a few of the mostdeformed symplectic basis states that span only a small fraction of the fullmodel space. The results are nearly independent of whether the bare orrenormalized effective interactions are used in the analysis. The outcomeconfirms Elliott's \SU{3} model which underpins the symplectic scheme, andabove all, points to the relevance of a symplectic no-core shell model that canreproduce experimental B(E2) values without effective charges as well asdeformed spatial modes associated with clustering phenomena in nuclei.
label: human

text: Evidence for symplectic symmetry in light nuclei is investigated within the ab initio no-core shell model (NCSM) framework. By analyzing wave functions obtained from realistic nucleon–nucleon interactions, we demonstrate that a small number of symplectic Sp(3,R) irreducible representations dominate the low-lying spectra and electromagnetic observables. This dominance persists across variations in model-space size and interaction details, indicating that symplectic symmetry is an emergent, robust organizational principle in these systems. Our results suggest that exploiting this symmetry can lead to more efficient many-body calculations and provide deeper insight into collective nuclear dynamics from first principles.
label: llm

text: The paper is considering an opportunity for the CERN/GranSasso (CNGS)neutrino complex, concurrent time-wise with T2K and NOvA, to search fortheta_13 oscillations and CP violation. Compared with large water Cherenkov(T2K) and fine grained scintillators (NOvA), the LAr-TPC offers a higherdetection efficiency and a lower backgrounds, since virtually all channels maybe unambiguously recognized. The present proposal, called MODULAr, describes a20 kt fiducial volume LAr-TPC, following very closely the technology developedfor the ICARUS-T60o, and is focused on the following activities, for which weseek an extended international collaboration:  (1) the neutrino beam from the CERN 400 GeV proton beam and an optimised hornfocussing, eventually with an increased intensity in the framework of the LHCaccelerator improvement program;  (2) A new experimental area LNGS-B, of at least 50000 m3 at 10 km off-axisfrom the main Laboratory, eventually upgradable to larger sizes. A location isunder consideration at about 1.2 km equivalent water depth;  (3) A new LAr Imaging detector of at least 20 kt fiducial mass. Such anincrease in the volume over the current ICARUS T600 needs to be carefullyconsidered. It is concluded that a very large mass is best realised with a setof many identical, independent units, each of 5 kt, "cloning" the technology ofthe T600. Further phases may foresee extensions of MODULAr to meet futurephysics goals.  The experiment might reasonably be operational in about 4/5 years, provided anew hall is excavated in the vicinity of the Gran Sasso Laboratory and adequatefunding and participation are made available.
label: human

text: A new, very massive modular Liquid Argon Imaging Chamber (MODULAr) is proposed to detect low-energy off-axis neutrinos from the CERN Neutrinos to Gran Sasso (CNGS) beam. The detector concept is based on a scalable array of industrially produced Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LAr-TPC) modules optimized for fine-grained imaging and efficient neutrino event reconstruction. By positioning the apparatus off-axis with respect to the CNGS beam, the neutrino energy spectrum is tuned toward lower energies, enhancing sensitivity to oscillation phenomena in the atmospheric mass-squared difference region. The modular design allows a progressive increase of the fiducial mass to the 20–100 kton scale, while maintaining manageable cryogenic, mechanical, and readout requirements. Advanced charge readout and light detection systems are envisaged to provide excellent spatial resolution, calorimetric performance, and background rejection capabilities. The project builds upon the operational experience of previous LAr-TPC experiments and leverages existing underground infrastructure to reduce cost and technical risk. Physics goals include precision measurements of νμ→ντ and νμ→νe appearance, improved constraints on oscillation parameters, and the exploration of sub-dominant effects such as CP violation in the lepton sector. This article outlines the detector concept, expected performance, and physics reach, and discusses the key R&D steps required to realize the MODULAr project.
label: llm

text: We present the results of a visible spectroscopic and photometric survey ofJupiter Trojans belonging to different dynamical families carried out at theESO-NTT telescope. We obtained data on 47 objects, 23 belonging to the L5 swarmand 24 to the L4 one. These data together with those already published byFornasier et al. (2004a) and Dotto et al. (2006), constitute a total sample ofvisible spectra for 80 objects. The survey allows us to investigate sixfamilies (Aneas, Anchises, Misenus, Phereclos, Sarpedon, Panthoos) in the L5cloud and four L4 families (Eurybates, Menelaus, 1986 WD and 1986 TS6). Thesample that we measured is dominated by D--type asteroids, with the exceptionof the Eurybates family in the L4 swarm, where there is a dominance of C- andP-type asteroids. All the spectra that we obtained are featureless with theexception of some Eurybates members, where a drop--off of the reflectance isdetected shortward of 5200 A. Similar features are seen in main belt C-typeasteroids and commonly attributed to the intervalence charge transfertransition in oxidized iron. Our sample comprises fainter and smaller Trojansas compared to the literature's data and allows us to investigate theproperties of objects with estimated diameter smaller than 40--50 km. Theanalysis of the spectral slopes and colors versus the estimated diameters showsthat the blue and red objects have indistinguishable size distribution. Weperform a statistical investigation of the Trojans's spectra propertydistributions as a function of their orbital and physical parameters, and incomparison with other classes of minor bodies in the outer Solar System.Trojans at lower inclination appear significantly bluer than those at higherinclination, but this effect is strongly driven by the Eurybates family.
label: human

text: We present the final results of a comprehensive visible spectroscopic and photometric survey of dynamical families within the Jupiter Trojan population. Using a homogeneous data set collected over multiple observing runs with medium‑resolution spectrographs and broadband optical filters, we systematically characterize the surface properties of family and non‑family Trojans. Our sample includes members of all major dynamical families in both L4 and L5 swarms, spanning a wide range of sizes, orbital inclinations, and libration amplitudes. We derive spectral slopes, taxonomic classifications in the visible range, and color indices, and we compare these properties across individual families and between the two Trojan clouds. The analysis confirms that most family members exhibit predominantly featureless, red to moderately red spectra typical of D‑type and P‑type asteroids, with only a minor fraction showing less reddish or neutral slopes. Several large, well‑defined families display statistically significant internal homogeneity in spectral slope and color, supporting a common collisional origin and compositionally coherent parent bodies. Conversely, other families show broader dispersions in optical properties, suggesting either partial interlopers, more complex collisional histories, or subsequent surface evolution processes. We find no compelling evidence for systematic differences in visible spectral behavior between L4 and L5 families when controlling for size and dynamical parameters. However, subtle trends with inclination and family age emerge, consistent with space weathering and impact resurfacing acting over Gyr timescales. By combining our dataset with updated dynamical clustering analyses, we identify new candidate family members and refine the membership of several previously known families.
label: llm

text: According to extensive experimental findings, the Ginzburg temperature$t_{G}$ for ionic fluids differs substantially from that of nonionic fluids[Schr\"oer W., Weig\"{a}rtner H. 2004 {\it Pure Appl. Chem.} {\bf 76} 19]. Atheoretical investigation of this outcome is proposed here by a mean fieldanalysis of the interplay of short and long range interactions on the value of$t_{G}$. We consider a quite general continuous charge-asymmetric model made ofcharged hard spheres with additional short-range interactions (withoutelectrostatic interactions the model belongs to the same universality class asthe 3D Ising model). The effective Landau-Ginzburg Hamiltonian of the fullsystem near its gas-liquid critical point is derived from which the Ginzburgtemperature is calculated as a function of the ionicity. The results obtainedin this way for $t_{G}$ are in good qualitative and sufficient quantitativeagreement with available experimental data.
label: human

text: Coulomb interactions fundamentally alter the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of fluids, giving rise to distinctive crossover behavior between short- and long-range dominated regimes. In this work, we investigate the crossover in a class of model ionic and dipolar fluids by combining analytical scaling arguments with large-scale molecular simulations. We derive effective field-theoretic descriptions that capture the interplay between Coulombic screening, density fluctuations, and critical phenomena near phase transitions. Our results show that the presence of long-range electrostatic forces modifies universal scaling functions and leads to nontrivial renormalization of effective interaction ranges as temperature, density, and ionic strength are varied. We identify characteristic crossover scales that separate regimes governed by mean-field-like behavior from those displaying Ising-type criticality, and we quantify how these scales depend on microscopic parameters such as charge valency and dielectric constant.
label: llm

text: The validity of the DFT models implemented by FIREBALL for CNT electronicdevice modeling is assessed. The effective masses, band gaps, and transmissioncoefficients of semi-conducting, zigzag, (n,0) carbon nanotubes (CNTs)resulting from the ab initio tight-binding density functional theory (DFT) codeFIREBALL and the empirical, nearest-neighbor pi-bond model are compared for allsemiconducting n values 5 <(=) n <(=) 35. The DFT values for the effectivemasses differ from the pi-bond values by +(-) 9% over the range of n values, 17<(=) n <(=) 29, most important for electronic device applications. Over therange 13 <(=) n <(=) 35, the DFT bandgaps are less than the empirical bandgapsby 20-180 meV depending on the functional and the n value. The pi-bond modelgives results that differ signifcantly from the DFT results when the CNTdiameter goes below 1 nm due to the large curvature of the CNT. The pi-bondmodel quickly becomes inaccurate away from the bandedges for a (10, 0) CNT, andit is completely inaccurate for n <(=) 8.
label: human

text: We investigate the electronic properties of single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) using both density functional theory (DFT) and an empirical π-bond tight-binding model. Systematic calculations are performed for nanotubes of varying chiralities and diameters to elucidate the relationship between geometrical structure and electronic band structure. The DFT results, obtained with generalized gradient approximation exchange-correlation functionals, serve as a benchmark for assessing the accuracy of the empirical π-bond model. We find that the π-bond model reproduces the qualitative features of the band structure and band gap for a wide range of nanotubes, but exhibits quantitative deviations for small-diameter and highly curved tubes. These deviations are analyzed in terms of curvature-induced σ–π hybridization and many-body effects that are not fully captured in the empirical model. Our study provides criteria for the reliable use of the π-bond model and offers guidance for the selection of theoretical approaches in the design and interpretation of carbon nanotube-based electronic devices.
label: llm

text: We carry out cosmological chemodynamical simulations with different strengthsof supernova (SN) feedback and study how galactic winds from star-forminggalaxies affect the features of hydrogen (HI) and metal (CIV and OVI)absorption systems in the intergalactic medium at high redshift. We find thatthe outflows tend to escape to low density regions, and hardly affect the densefilaments visible in HI absorption. As a result, the strength of HI absorptionnear galaxies is not reduced by galactic winds, but even slightly increases. Wealso find that a lack of HI absorption for lines of sight (LOS) close togalaxies, as found by Adelberger et al., can be created by hot gas around thegalaxies induced by accretion shock heating. In contrast to HI, metalabsorption systems are sensitive to the presence of winds. The models withoutfeedback can produce the strong CIV and OVI absorption lines in LOS within 50kpc from galaxies, while strong SN feedback is capable of creating strong CIVand OVI lines out to about twice that distance. We also analyze the meantransmissivity of HI, CIV, and OVI within 1 h$^{-1}$ Mpc from star-forminggalaxies. The probability distribution of the transmissivity of HI isindependent of the strength of SN feedback, but strong feedback produces LOSwith lower transmissivity of metal lines. Additionally, strong feedback canproduce strong OVI lines even in cases where HI absorption is weak. We concludethat OVI is probably the best tracer for galactic winds at high redshift.
label: human

text: Galactic-scale winds are believed to play a critical role in regulating star formation and distributing metals into the intergalactic medium at early cosmic times. In this work, we investigate the observable signatures of galactic winds around high-redshift (z ≳ 2) galaxies using a combination of cosmological hydrodynamical simulations and radiative transfer modeling. We focus on the spatial and kinematic properties of gas traced by resonant and non-resonant transitions, including Lyα, C IV, and Si II, in both emission and absorption. Our analysis demonstrates that outflows produce characteristic blue-shifted absorption and redshifted emission features whose strengths and profiles depend sensitively on wind geometry, mass-loading, and viewing angle. We show that extended Lyα halos, with surface brightness profiles declining on scales of tens of kiloparsecs, naturally arise from resonant scattering in outflowing media. The simulations reproduce key aspects of observed circumgalactic absorption line statistics, including enhanced metal-line covering fractions and velocity spreads around star-forming galaxies. We find that the incidence and detectability of wind signatures are strongly correlated with instantaneous star formation rate and galaxy stellar mass. By forward-modeling mock observations with realistic instrumental effects, we provide predictions for current and upcoming spectroscopic surveys targeting the circumgalactic medium at high redshift. Our results imply that a significant fraction of the enriched intergalactic medium at z ∼ 2–4 can be directly linked to past episodes of strong galactic winds.
label: llm

text: This paper deals with the investigation of the solution of an unifiedfractional reaction-diffusion equation associated with the Caputo derivative asthe time-derivative and Riesz-Feller fractional derivative as thespace-derivative. The solution is derived by the application of the Laplace andFourier transforms in closed form in terms of the H-function. The resultsderived are of general nature and include the results investigated earlier bymany authors, notably by Mainardi et al. (2001, 2005) for the fundamentalsolution of the space-time fractional diffusion equation, and Saxena et al.(2006a, b) for fractional reaction- diffusion equations. The advantage of usingRiesz-Feller derivative lies in the fact that the solution of the fractionalreaction-diffusion equation containing this derivative includes the fundamentalsolution for space-time fractional diffusion, which itself is a generalizationof neutral fractional diffusion, space-fractional diffusion, andtime-fractional diffusion. These specialized types of diffusion can beinterpreted as spatial probability density functions evolving in time and areexpressible in terms of the H-functions in compact form.
label: human

text: This paper investigates analytical solutions of fractional reaction-diffusion equations expressed in terms of the Fox H-function. We consider a broad class of space-time fractional equations involving Caputo time derivatives and Riesz–Feller space derivatives to model anomalous diffusion coupled with nonlinear reaction terms. By applying Laplace and Fourier transform techniques, we derive exact solution representations in closed form involving the H-function, which unifies and generalizes many special functions used in diffusion theory. The derived solutions accommodate diverse boundary and initial conditions, including localized and power-law distributed initial data, and recover classical diffusion and reaction-diffusion solutions as limiting cases. Asymptotic behavior and scaling properties of the solutions are analyzed via known identities and asymptotic expansions of the H-function. These results reveal the impact of fractional orders and skewness parameters on propagation speed, front formation, and long-time tails of the concentration profiles. The presented framework provides a unified mathematical tool for treating a wide variety of anomalous reaction-diffusion processes in physics, biology, and engineering.
label: llm

text: During the epoch of reionization, the formation of radiation sources isaccompanied by the growth of a H- photodissociating flux. We estimate theimpact of this flux on the formation of molecular hydrogen and cooling in thefirst galaxies, assuming different types of radiation sources (e.g. Pop II andPop III stars, miniquasars). We find that H- photodissociation reduces theformation of H2 molecules by a factor of ~1+1000k_s*x/(f_esc*delta), where x isthe mean ionized fraction in the IGM, f_esc is the fraction of ionizing photonsthat escape from their progenitor halos, delta is the local gas overdensity andk_s is an order unity constant which depends on the type of radiation source.By the time a significant fraction of the universe becomes ionized, H-photodissociation may significantly reduce the H2 abundance and, with it, theprimordial star formation rate, delaying the progress of reionization.
label: human

text: We investigate the impact of the first ionizing radiation sources on the formation of molecular hydrogen via the photodissociation of the intermediate species H⁻ in the early universe. Using detailed radiative transfer calculations coupled with primordial gas chemistry, we quantify how soft UV and X-ray backgrounds from Population III stars and miniquasars regulate the H⁻ abundance and thereby suppress H₂ formation in minihalos. We show that even relatively weak radiation fields can significantly reduce H₂ cooling, delaying star formation in low-mass halos and modifying the characteristic mass scale of the first luminous objects. Our results highlight H⁻ photodissociation as a key negative feedback mechanism in cosmological structure formation and provide updated constraints for models of early star and galaxy formation.
label: llm

text: Prices of commodities or assets produce what is called time-series. Differentkinds of financial time-series have been recorded and studied for decades.Nowadays, all transactions on a financial market are recorded, leading to ahuge amount of data available, either for free in the Internet or commercially.Financial time-series analysis is of great interest to practitioners as well asto theoreticians, for making inferences and predictions. Furthermore, thestochastic uncertainties inherent in financial time-series and the theoryneeded to deal with them make the subject especially interesting not only toeconomists, but also to statisticians and physicists. While it would be aformidable task to make an exhaustive review on the topic, with this review wetry to give a flavor of some of its aspects.
label: human

text: Financial time-series analysis focuses on the statistical properties and dynamic behavior of asset prices, returns, and related financial variables observed over time. This brief overview highlights key concepts such as stationarity, autocorrelation, volatility clustering, and the presence of heavy tails in financial data. Methodological approaches including ARIMA models, GARCH-type volatility models, and more recent machine learning techniques are discussed in the context of modeling, forecasting, and risk management. The article concludes by outlining current challenges, such as handling high-frequency data and structural breaks, and suggests directions for future research in financial econometrics.
label: llm

text: We consider a system composed of a trapped atom and a trapped ion. The ioncharge induces in the atom an electric dipole moment, which attracts it with anr^{-4} dependence at large distances. In the regime considered here, thecharacteristic range of the atom-ion interaction is comparable or larger thanthe characteristic size of the trapping potential, which excludes theapplication of the contact pseudopotential. The short-range part of theinteraction is described in the framework of quantum-defect theory, byintroducing some short-range parameters, which can be related to the s-wavescattering length. When the separation between traps is changed we observetrap-induced shape resonances between molecular bound states and vibrationalstates of the external trapping potential. Our analysis is extended toquasi-one-dimensional geometries, when the scattering exhibitconfinement-induced resonances, similar to the ones studied before forshort-range interactions. For quasi-one-dimensional systems we investigate theeffects of coupling between the center of mass and relative motion, whichoccurs for different trapping frequencies of atom and ion traps. Finally, weshow how the two types of resonances can be employed for quantum state controland spectroscopy of atom-ion molecules.
label: human

text: Controlled collisions between individual atoms and ions provide a powerful platform for studying fundamental quantum interactions and for developing hybrid quantum technologies. In this work, we theoretically and experimentally investigate collisions between a single neutral atom and a single ion that are guided and brought into contact by movable trapping potentials. We employ dynamically reconfigurable optical and radio-frequency traps to position and transport the particles with sub-micrometer precision while maintaining quantum-level control of their motional states. By tailoring the temporal trajectories of the trapping potentials, we realize tunable collision energies spanning from the ultracold s-wave regime to the onset of higher partial waves. We characterize the collisions through measurements of elastic and inelastic scattering rates, energy-dependent cross sections, and state-changing processes, and compare them to quantum scattering calculations including the long-range atom–ion polarization interaction. Our results demonstrate that controlled transport protocols can be used to engineer the collisional phase and to selectively enhance or suppress particular scattering channels. We further show that the movable potentials enable repeated, programmable collisions between the same atom–ion pair.
label: llm

text: We present in this article a detailed quantitative discussion of themeasurement of the leptonic mixing angle theta_13 through currently scheduledreactor neutrino oscillation experiments. We thus focus on Double Chooz (PhaseI & II), Daya Bay (Phase I & II) and RENO experiments. We perform a unifiedanalysis, including systematics, backgrounds and accurate experimental setup ineach case. Each identified systematic error and background impact has beenassessed on experimental setups following published data when available andextrapolating from Double Chooz acquired knowledge otherwise. After reviewingthe experiments, we present a new analysis of their sensitivities to sin^2(2theta_13) and study the impact of the different systematics based on the pullsapproach. Through this generic statistical analysis we discuss the advantagesand drawbacks of each experimental setup.
label: human

text: A unified analysis of the reactor neutrino program provides a comprehensive framework for extracting the mixing angle θ\(_{13}\) from current and past reactor experiments. In this work, we combine data from short- and medium-baseline reactor neutrino measurements, incorporating a consistent treatment of flux predictions, detector response, and systematic uncertainties. We develop a global statistical methodology that accounts for correlations among experiments and between different sources of error, allowing a robust determination of θ\(_{13}\). Special attention is paid to reactor flux normalization, fuel-evolution effects, and background modeling, which are identified as dominant limitations in existing analyses. Applying our framework to the combined data set, we obtain updated constraints on sin\(^2\)(2θ\(_{13}\)) and assess the internal consistency of the reactor neutrino program.
label: llm

text: We present a theoretical framework for plasma turbulence in astrophysicalplasmas (solar wind, interstellar medium, galaxy clusters, accretion disks).The key assumptions are that the turbulence is anisotropic with respect to themean magnetic field and frequencies are low compared to the ion cyclotronfrequency. The energy injected at the outer scale scale has to be convertedinto heat, which ultimately cannot be done without collisions. A KINETICCASCADE develops that brings the energy to collisional scales both in space andvelocity. Its nature depends on the physics of plasma fluctuations. In each ofthe physically distinct scale ranges, the kinetic problem is systematicallyreduced to a more tractable set of equations. In the "inertial range" above theion gyroscale, the kinetic cascade splits into a cascade of Alfvenicfluctuations, which are governed by the RMHD equations at both the collisionaland collisionless scales, and a passive cascade of compressive fluctuations,which obey a linear kinetic equation along the moving field lines associatedwith the Alfvenic component. In the "dissipation range" between the ion andelectron gyroscales, there are again two cascades: the kinetic-Alfven-wave(KAW) cascade governed by two fluid-like Electron RMHD equations and a passivephase-space cascade of ion entropy fluctuations. The latter cascade brings theenergy of the inertial-range fluctuations that was damped by collisionlesswave-particle interaction at the ion gyroscale to collisional scales in thephase space and leads to ion heating. The KAW energy is similarly damped at theelectron gyroscale and converted into electron heat. Kolmogorov-style scalingrelations are derived for these cascades. Astrophysical and space-physicalapplications are discussed in detail.
label: human

text: Astrophysical gyrokinetics provides a rigorous framework for describing turbulent cascades in magnetized, weakly collisional plasmas across a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. In this work, we develop a unified theory that connects kinetic and fluid regimes of plasma turbulence via anisotropic cascades constrained by strong background magnetic fields. We derive the gyrokinetic equations appropriate for low-frequency, small-amplitude fluctuations and elucidate the ordering assumptions relevant to astrophysical environments such as the solar wind, intracluster medium, and accretion flows. Using these equations, we systematically distinguish between fluid-like magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence at large scales and kinetic Alfvén and compressive cascades at sub-ion-Larmor scales. We demonstrate how energy injected at large scales via MHD motions is transferred through an anisotropic cascade into kinetic scales where it is ultimately dissipated by collisionless mechanisms. The role of Landau damping, transit-time damping, and stochastic heating in mediating the conversion of turbulent electromagnetic energy into particle heat is analyzed within the gyrokinetic formalism. We identify distinct inertial ranges in both perpendicular and parallel wavenumbers and show how critical balance shapes the spectral distribution of turbulent energy. Reduced fluid models derived from gyrokinetics are employed to characterize regimes where fluid approximations remain valid and to quantify departures from MHD behavior. We compare theoretical predictions with numerical simulations and in situ spacecraft observations, highlighting agreements in spectral slopes, anisotropy, and dissipation signatures. Implications for plasma heating, thermal balance, and nonthermal particle acceleration in astrophysical systems are discussed.
label: llm

text: We propose the Z -> gamma gamma decay, a process strictly forbidden in thestandard model, as a signal suitable for the search of noncommutativity ofcoordinates at very short distances. We compute the Z -> gamma gamma partialwidthin the framework of the recently proposed renormalizable gauge sector ofthe noncommutative standard model. The one-loop renormalizability is obtainedfor the model containing the usual six representations of matter fields of thefirst generation. Even more, the noncommutative part is finite or free ofdivergences, showing that perhaps new interaction symmetry exists in thenoncommutative gauge sector of the model. Discovery of such symmetry would beof tremendous importance in further search for the violation of the Lorentzinvariance at very high energies. Experimental possibilities of Z -> gammagamma decay are analyzed and a firm bound to the scale of the noncommutativityparameter is set around 1 TeV.
label: human

text: In this work we investigate the rare decay process \(Z \rightarrow \gamma\gamma\) as a potential signal of space-time noncommutativity within the framework of the renormalizable gauge sector of the \(\theta\)-expanded Noncommutative Standard Model (NCSM). Starting from a Seiberg–Witten map-expanded action, we derive the effective gauge boson interactions to first order in the noncommutativity parameter \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) and identify the Lorentz- and CPT-violating structures that mediate the forbidden \(Z \rightarrow \gamma\gamma\) decay. We perform a one-loop renormalization analysis of the gauge sector and show that, for a specific choice of deformation parameters, the theory remains renormalizable while inducing finite and predictive corrections to the trilinear neutral gauge couplings. On this basis, we compute the decay amplitude and width for \(Z \rightarrow \gamma\gamma\), emphasizing their explicit dependence on the components of \(\theta^{\mu\nu}\) and the noncommutative energy scale \(\Lambda_{\text{NC}}\).
label: llm

text: In this article we analyze the impact of B-physics and Higgs physics at LEPon standard and non-standard Higgs bosons searches at the Tevatron and the LHC,within the framework of minimal flavor violating supersymmetric models. TheB-physics constraints we consider come from the experimental measurements ofthe rare B-decays b -> s gamma and B_u -> tau nu and the experimental limit onthe B_s -> mu+ mu- branching ratio. We show that these constraints are severefor large values of the trilinear soft breaking parameter A_t, rendering thenon-standard Higgs searches at hadron colliders less promising. On the contrarythese bounds are relaxed for small values of A_t and large values of theHiggsino mass parameter mu, enhancing the prospects for the direct detection ofnon-standard Higgs bosons at both colliders. We also consider the availableATLAS and CMS projected sensitivities in the standard model Higgs searchchannels, and we discuss the LHC's ability in probing the whole MSSM parameterspace. In addition we also consider the expected Tevatron collidersensitivities in the standard model Higgs h -> b bbar channel to show that itmay be able to find 3 sigma evidence in the B-physics allowed regions for smallor moderate values of the stop mixing parameter.
label: human

text: Searches for Higgs bosons in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM) at hadron colliders face a number of theoretical and experimental challenges. The extended Higgs sector, characterized by additional neutral and charged states, leads to a rich but complex phenomenology with many overlapping signatures. Radiative corrections, dependence on supersymmetric parameters, and uncertainties in parton distribution functions significantly affect production cross sections and branching ratios, complicating precise predictions. Experimentally, large QCD backgrounds, limited mass resolution, and the need for specialized triggers hinder the separation of MSSM Higgs signals from Standard Model processes. We review the impact of benchmark scenarios, flavor and CP-violating effects, and invisible or non-standard decay modes on current and future search strategies at the LHC and beyond. Finally, we discuss how combined analyses, improved theoretical calculations, and upgraded detector capabilities can mitigate these challenges and enhance the discovery or exclusion reach for MSSM Higgs bosons.
label: llm

text: Kination dominated quintessence models of dark energy have the intriguingfeature that the relic abundance of thermal cold dark matter can besignificantly enhanced compared to the predictions from standard cosmology.Previous treatments of such models do not include a realistic embedding ofinflationary initial conditions. We remedy this situation by constructing aviable inflationary model in which the inflaton and quintessence field are thesame scalar degree of freedom. Kination domination is achieved after inflationthrough a strong push or "kick" of the inflaton, and sufficient reheating canbe achieved depending on model parameters. This allows us to explore bothmodel-dependent and model-independent cosmological predictions of thisscenario. We find that measurements of the B-mode CMB polarization can rule outthis class of scenarios almost model independently. We also discuss otherexperimentally accessible signatures for this class of models.
label: human

text: This article explores an inflationary cosmology framework that unifies the phenomena of dark energy and dark matter within a single theoretical model. By extending the standard inflationary paradigm, we propose a mechanism in which the inflaton field dynamics generate relic components that can simultaneously account for the observed dark matter abundance and the accelerated expansion of the universe. We develop a formalism linking the inflaton potential parameters to late-time cosmological observables, providing testable predictions for cosmic microwave background anisotropies and large-scale structure formation. The model offers a natural explanation for the coincidence problem by intrinsically relating the energy scales of dark matter and dark energy through inflationary physics. Numerical simulations demonstrate consistency with current observational constraints from Planck and Type Ia supernovae data. Our results suggest that early-universe inflation not only drives initial expansion but may also fundamentally underpin the dark sector phenomena shaping cosmic evolution.
label: llm

text: The charge transport mechanism and the macroscopic dielectric constant inpolycrystalline device materials commonly exhibit several components such aselectrode-sample interface, grain boundary and bulk contributions. In order togain precise understanding of the functionality of polycrystallineelectroceramic device materials it is essential to deconvolute thesecontributions. The paradigm of functional thermistor ceramics based on thickfilm spinel manganates has been studied by temperature dependent alternatingcurrent impedance spectroscopy. Three typical relaxation phenomena weredetected, which all showed a separated temperature dependence of resistivityconsistent with thermally activated charge transport. The dominating grainboundary and the interface contributions exhibited distinctively differentcapacitance allowing clear identification. The composite nature of thedielectric properties in polycrystalline functional ceramics was emphasized,and impedance spectroscopy was shown to be a powerful tool to account for andmodel such behaviour.
label: human

text: This study investigates the temperature and frequency dependent impedance characteristics of electroceramic functional oxide thermistors. Comprehensive impedance spectroscopy measurements were conducted across a broad temperature range and varying frequencies to elucidate the complex electrical response mechanisms. The results reveal distinct impedance behaviors associated with grain boundary and bulk contributions, which evolve significantly with temperature. Frequency-dependent analysis demonstrates the dispersive nature of charge transport and relaxation phenomena within the thermistor material. Additionally, the correlation between impedance parameters and thermistor performance metrics is examined to inform device optimization. These findings provide critical insights into the fundamental electrochemical processes governing oxide thermistor functionality and contribute to the advancement of temperature sensing technologies.
label: llm

text: The CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) experiment searches for axions from theSun converted into photons with energies up to around 10 keV via the inversePrimakoff effect in the high magnetic field of a superconducting Large HadronCollider (LHC) prototype magnet. A backside illuminated pn-CCD detector inconjunction with an X-ray mirror optics is one of the three detectors used inCAST to register the expected photon signal. Since this signal is very rare anddifferent background components (environmental gamma radiation, cosmic rays,intrinsic radioactive impurities in the set-up, ...) entangle it, a detailedstudy of the detector background has been undertaken with the aim to understandand further reduce the background level of the detector. The analysis is basedon measured data taken during the Phase I of CAST and on Monte Carlosimulations of different background components. This study will show that theobserved background level (at a rate of (8.00+-0.07)10^-5 counts/cm^2/s/keVbetween 1 and 7 keV) seems to be dominated by the external gamma background dueto usual activities at the experimental site, while radioactive impurities inthe detector itself and cosmic neutrons could make just smaller contribution.
label: human

text: This study presents a comprehensive background analysis of the pn-CCD detector employed in the CERN Axion Solar Telescope (CAST) experiment. We investigate the intrinsic and environmental noise sources affecting the detector’s performance, with an emphasis on their impact on data quality and signal sensitivity. Detailed characterization of the detector’s response to various background radiation components was carried out using calibration measurements and Monte Carlo simulations. The results provide key insights into optimizing the detector setup and data processing strategies to minimize background interference. These findings contribute to enhancing the CAST experiment’s capability in the search for solar axions and improving the reliability of its detection results.
label: llm

text: Phase closure at 682 GHz and 691 GHz was first achieved using three antennasof the Submillimeter Array (SMA) interferometer located on Mauna Kea, Hawaii.Initially, phase closure was demonstrated at 682.5 GHz on Sept. 19, 2002 usingan artificial ground-based "beacon" signal. Subsequently, astronomicaldetections of both Saturn and Uranus were made at the frequency of the CO(6-5)transition (691.473 GHz) on all three baselines on Sept. 22, 2002. While thelarger planets such as Saturn are heavily resolved even on these shortbaselines (25.2m, 25.2m and 16.4m), phase closure was achieved on Uranus andCallisto. This was the first successful experiment to obtain phase closure inthis frequency band. The CO(6-5) line was also detected towards Orion BN/KL andother Galactic sources, as was the vibrationally-excited 658 GHz water maserline toward evolved stars. We present these historic detections, as well as thefirst arcsecond-scale images obtained in this frequency band.
label: human

text: We report on the successful measurement of phase closure at 691 GHz using the Submillimeter Array (SMA), marking a significant advancement in high-frequency interferometric techniques. This work demonstrates the capability of the SMA to perform accurate phase calibration at submillimeter wavelengths, a crucial step for improving image fidelity in this challenging regime. Our observations utilized bright celestial sources and incorporated specialized calibration strategies to mitigate atmospheric and instrumental phase instabilities. The results confirm that reliable closure phases can be obtained at 691 GHz, enabling more precise imaging and characterization of compact astrophysical objects. We also discuss the implications of these findings for future high-resolution studies of star formation regions, protoplanetary disks, and extragalactic sources. This study paves the way for utilizing the SMA and similar instruments at even higher frequencies with enhanced calibration methods.
label: llm

text: A new inflationary scenario whose exponential potential $V(\Phi)$ has aquadratic dependence on the field $\Phi$ in addition to the standard linearterm is confronted with the tree-year observations of the Wilkinson-MicrowaveAnisotropy Probe and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey data. The number of e-folds($N$), the ratio of tensor-to-scalar perturbations ($r$), the spectral scalarindex of the primordial power spectrum ($n_s$) and its running ($dn_s/d\ln k$)depend on the dimensionless parameter $\alpha$ multiplying the quadratic termin the potential. In the limit $\alpha \to 0$ all the results of the standardexponential potential are fully recovered. For values of $\alpha \neq 0$, wefind that the model predictions are in good agreement with the currentobservations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) anisotropies andLarge-Scale Structure (LSS) in the Universe.
label: human

text: We investigate constraints on a single-field inflationary model by analyzing data from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) and Large-Scale Structure (LSS) observations. Using the latest measurements from Planck and large-scale galaxy surveys, we perform a joint likelihood analysis to tightly constrain the model parameters that govern the inflationary potential. Our results show that the combined CMB and LSS data significantly reduce the permissible parameter space, providing strong evidence in favor of slow-roll inflation consistent with a nearly scale-invariant power spectrum. These findings highlight the power of integrating cosmological probes to refine our understanding of the inflationary epoch and the origin of cosmic structure.
label: llm

text: We examine the optical emission line properties of Brightest Cluster Galaxies(BCGs) selected from two large, homogeneous datasets. The first is the X-rayselected National Optical Astronomy Observatory Fundamental Plane Survey(NFPS), and the second is the C4 catalogue of optically selected clusters builtfrom the Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release ~3 (SDSS DR3). Our goal is tobetter understand the optical line emission in BCGs with respect to propertiesof the galaxy and the host cluster. Throughout the analysis we compare the lineemission of the BCGs to that of a control sample made of the other brightgalaxies near the cluster centre. Overall, both the NFPS and SDSS show a modestfraction of BCGs with emission lines (~15%). No trend in the fraction ofemitting BCGs as a function of galaxy mass or cluster velocity dispersion isfound. However we find that, for those BCGs found in cooling flow clusters,71^{+9}_{-14}% have optical emission. Furthermore, if we consider only BCGswithin 50kpc of the X-ray centre of a cooling flow cluster, the emission-linefraction rises further to 100^{+0}_{-15}%. Excluding the cooling flow clusters,only ~10% of BCGs are line emitting, comparable to the control sample ofgalaxies. We show that the physical origin of the emission line activityvaries: in some cases it has LINER-like line ratios, whereas in others it is acomposite of star-formation and LINER-like activity. We conclude that thepresence of emission lines in BCGs is directly related to the cooling of X-raygas at the cluster centre.
label: human

text: This study investigates the properties and origins of line emission in the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) identified within the NOAO Fundamental Plane Survey and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. We analyze spectroscopic data to characterize emission line strengths, ionization mechanisms, and kinematic features across a representative sample of BCGs. Our results demonstrate that a substantial fraction of BCGs exhibit significant emission lines, indicative of ongoing star formation or active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. Comparisons between the two surveys reveal consistent trends in line ratios, suggesting similar underlying physical processes. We employ diagnostic diagrams to distinguish between photoionization by young stars and AGN-related excitation. The spatial distribution of emission lines within BCGs further supports a predominance of central AGN influence, although extended star-forming regions are also detected in some systems. We discuss the implications of emission line properties on the evolutionary pathways of BCGs and their role within galaxy cluster environments. Correlations between emission line luminosity and cluster properties underscore the impact of the intracluster medium on BCG activity. This work also explores how cooling flows and feedback mechanisms might regulate the observed emission. Our findings contribute to a more unified understanding of the diverse ionization sources in BCGs and their connection to cluster-scale processes. Finally, we highlight future avenues for high-resolution observations to disentangle complex excitation scenarios within these massive galaxies.
label: llm

text: We analyze several possibilities for precisely measuring electronictransitions in atomic helium by the direct use of phase-stabilized femtosecondfrequency combs. Because the comb is self-calibrating and can be shifted intothe ultraviolet spectral region via harmonic generation, it offers the prospectof greatly improved accuracy for UV and far-UV transitions. To take advantageof this accuracy an ultracold helium sample is needed. For measurements of thetriplet spectrum a magneto-optical trap (MOT) can be used to cool and trapmetastable 2^3S state atoms. We analyze schemes for measuring the two-photon$2^3S \to 4^3S$ interval, and for resonant two-photon excitation to highRydberg states, $2^3S \to 3^3P \to n^3S,D$. We also analyze experiments on thesinglet-state spectrum. To accomplish this we propose schemes for producing andtrapping ultracold helium in the 1^1S or 2^1S state via intercombinationtransitions. A particularly intriguing scenario is the possibility of measuringthe $1^1S \to 2^1S$ transition with extremely high accuracy by use oftwo-photon excitation in a magic wavelength trap that operates identically forboth states. We predict a ``triple magic wavelength'' at 412 nm that couldfacilitate numerous experiments on trapped helium atoms, because here thepolarizabilities of the 1^1S, 2^1S and 2^3S states are all similar, small, andpositive.
label: human

text: This article explores the potential advances in precision measurements of atomic helium enabled by direct frequency comb spectroscopy. Frequency combs provide a unique combination of high spectral resolution and broad bandwidth, facilitating unprecedented accuracy in spectroscopic studies. We review recent experimental progress in applying frequency comb technology to helium atoms, focusing on transition frequencies that are fundamental for testing quantum electrodynamics (QED) theories. The method allows direct excitation of helium’s electronic transitions with minimal systematic uncertainties, offering a pathway to improved determinations of fundamental constants. Our analysis assesses the challenges of controlling environmental and technical noise sources that affect measurement precision. We discuss the integration of frequency combs with atomic beam and trapped helium setups to optimize signal-to-noise ratios. Potential improvements in comb technology and detection schemes are examined, highlighting their impact on future measurement sensitivity. The prospects for refining helium energy level measurements could enable stringent tests of two-electron QED calculations and advance metrology standards. Ultimately, direct frequency comb spectroscopy stands as a promising tool to push the frontiers of atomic physics and precision measurement science.
label: llm

text: The mapping of time-dependent densities on potentials in quantum mechanics iscritically examined. The issue is of significance ever since Runge and Gross(Phys. Rev. Lett. 52, 997 (1984)) established the uniqueness of the mapping,forming a theoretical basis for time-dependent density functional theory. Weargue that besides existence (so called v-representability) and uniquenessthere is an important question of stability and chaos. Studying a 2-levelsystem we find innocent, almost constant densities that cannot be constructedfrom any potential (non-existence). We further show via a Lyapunov analysisthat the mapping of densities on potentials has chaotic regions in this case.In real space the situation is more subtle. V-representability is formallyassured but the mapping is often chaotic making the actual construction of thepotential almost impossible. The chaotic nature of the mapping, studied for thefirst time here, has serious consequences regarding the possibility of usingTDDFT in real-time settings.
label: human

text: This article investigates the fundamental problem of establishing a rigorous mapping between time-dependent electronic densities and the corresponding external potentials in quantum mechanics. Building on the framework of time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT), we analyze the conditions under which a unique potential can be associated with a given evolving density profile. We provide a detailed examination of the mathematical structures underlying this mapping, emphasizing the role of initial states and the domain of admissible densities. By extending previous existence and uniqueness theorems, we identify new constraints that ensure invertibility in broader contexts, including systems with complex boundary conditions. Our approach leverages functional analysis techniques to clarify the dependence of potentials on both density and initial wavefunction data. We also discuss practical implications for computational quantum chemistry, where accurate potential reconstruction is vital for predicting dynamical properties.
label: llm

text: Quantum gravity is analyzed from the viewpoint of the renormalization group.The analysis is based on methods introduced by J. Polchinski concerning theperturbative renormalization with flow equations. In the first part of thiswork, the program of renormalization with flow equations is reviewed and thenextended to effective field theories that have a finite UV cutoff. This is donefor a scalar field theory by imposing additional renormalization conditions forsome of the nonrenormalizable couplings. It turns out that one so obtains astatement on the predictivity of the effective theory at scales far below theUV cutoff. In particular, nonrenormalizable theories can be treated withoutproblems in the proposed framework. In the second part, the standard covariantBRS quantization program for Euclidean Einstein gravity is applied. A momentumcutoff regularization is imposed and the resulting violation of theSlavnov-Taylor identities is discussed. Deriving Polchinski's renormalizationgroup equation for Euclidean quantum gravity, the predictivity of effectivequantum gravity at scales far below the Planck scale is investigated with flowequations. A fine-tuning procedure for restoring the violated Slavnov-Tayloridentities is proposed and it is argued that in the effective quantum gravitycontext, the restoration will only be accomplished with finite accuracy.Finally, the no-cutoff limit of Euclidean quantum gravity is analyzed from theviewpoint of the Polchinski method. It is speculated whether a limit withnonvanishing gravitational constant might exist where the latter wouldultimatively be determined by the cosmological constant and the masses of theelementary particles.
label: human

text: This article explores the framework of renormalization within the context of General Relativity, focusing on the formulation and analysis of effective actions. We begin by reviewing the challenges inherent to quantizing gravity and the role of non-renormalizability in conventional perturbative approaches. Through the use of effective field theory techniques, we develop a systematic method to construct effective actions that capture gravitational dynamics at different energy scales. The study emphasizes the significance of scale-dependent coupling parameters and their flow under the renormalization group equations. We derive explicit expressions for one-loop corrections to the Einstein-Hilbert action and analyze their impact on low-energy gravitational phenomena. Our approach highlights the interplay between ultraviolet divergences and the necessity for introducing higher-derivative terms in the effective action. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these findings for the asymptotic safety program and the search for a consistent ultraviolet completion of gravity. By comparing our results with alternative quantization schemes, we clarify the physical interpretation of the effective action parameters. The paper also addresses potential observational consequences arising from modifications to classical General Relativity predicted by the effective action framework. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at extending this formalism to include matter fields and exploring its applications in cosmology and black hole physics.
label: llm

text: We present the first results from a new generation of simulated large skycoverage (~100 square degrees) Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (SZE) cluster surveysusing the cosmological adaptive mesh refinement N-body/hydro code Enzo. We havesimulated a very large (512^3h^{-3}Mpc^3) volume with unprecedented dynamicrange. We have generated simulated light cones to match the resolution andsensitivity of current and future SZE instruments. Unlike many previous studiesof this type, our simulation includes unbound gas, where an appreciablefraction of the baryons in the universe reside.  We have found that cluster line-of-sight overlap may be a significant issuein upcoming single-dish SZE surveys. Smaller beam surveys (~1 arcmin) have morethan one massive cluster within a beam diameter 5-10% of the time, and a largerbeam experiment like Planck has multiple clusters per beam 60% of the time. Weexplore the contribution of unresolved halos and unbound gas to the SZEsignature at the maximum decrement. We find that there is a contribution fromgas outside clusters of ~16% per object on average for upcoming surveys. Thisadds both bias and scatter to the deduced value of the integrated SZE, addingdifficulty in accurately calibrating a cluster Y-M relationship.  Finally, we find that in images where objects with M > 5x10^{13} M_{\odot}have had their SZE signatures removed, roughly a third of the total SZE fluxstill remains. This gas exists at least partially in the Warm Hot IntergalacticMedium (WHIM), and will possibly be detectable with the upcoming generation ofSZE surveys.
label: human

text: The Santa Fe Light Cone Simulation Project presents a comprehensive study addressing the challenges posed by confusion noise in upcoming Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (SZ) effect surveys. This first paper in the series focuses on the impact of the Warm-Hot Intergalactic Medium (WHIM) on the detectability and characterization of SZ signals from galaxy clusters. Employing state-of-the-art cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, we generate realistic light cone volumes that capture the complex interplay between large-scale structure and the diffuse baryonic component. Our analysis reveals that confusion from unresolved, low-mass structures and filamentary WHIM contributes significantly to the SZ background, complicating cluster identification in next-generation experiments. We implement advanced source extraction algorithms to quantify detection thresholds under varying survey parameters and noise conditions. The results indicate that WHIM-induced confusion can bias cluster mass estimates if not properly accounted for, leading to systematic uncertainties in cosmological constraints derived from SZ surveys. By comparing simulated SZ maps with and without WHIM contributions, we isolate its specific effects on the noise power spectrum and angular clustering signals. The study further explores strategies to mitigate confusion, including multi-frequency observations and joint analyses with complementary datasets such as X-ray and weak lensing measurements. Our findings highlight the necessity of incorporating realistic baryonic physics in survey simulations to optimize cluster detection pipelines.
label: llm

text: The physical properties of almost any kind of astronomical object can bederived by fitting synthetic spectra or photometry extracted from theoreticalmodels to observational data. This process usually involves working withmultiwavelength data, which is one of the cornerstones of the VO philosophy.  From this kind of studies, when combining with theoretical isochrones one caneven estimate ages. We present here the results obtained from a code designedto perform chi^2 tests to both spectroscopic models (or the associatedsynthetic photometry) and combinations of blackbodies (including modifiedblackbodies). Some steps in this process can already be done in a VOenvironment, and the rest are in the process of development. We must note thatthis kind of studies in star forming regions, clusters, etc. produce a hugeamount of data, very tedious to analyze using the traditional methodology. Thismake them excellent examples where to apply the VO capabilities.
label: human

text: This article explores the methodologies and challenges involved in characterizing cool astrophysical objects through spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting techniques, with a particular focus on age estimation. Cool objects, such as brown dwarfs and exoplanets, exhibit complex atmospheres and spectra that require sophisticated modeling approaches to accurately interpret their observed SEDs. We review current state-of-the-art fitting methods that integrate photometric and spectroscopic data across multiple wavelengths to constrain fundamental parameters including temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity. Emphasis is placed on the interplay between model atmospheres and evolutionary tracks, which together enable the derivation of reliable age estimates for these objects. We discuss the sources of uncertainty in both the observational data and theoretical models, highlighting the limitations they impose on age determination. Case studies of representative cool objects illustrate how advancements in SED fitting have improved constraints on their physical and temporal properties.
label: llm

text: This paper uses firm-level data recorded in the AMADEUS database toinvestigate the distribution of labour productivity in different Europeancountries. We find that the upper tail of the empirical productivitydistributions follows a decaying power-law, whose exponent $\alpha$ is obtainedby a semi-parametric estimation technique recently developed by Clementi et al.(2006). The emergence of "fat tails" in productivity distribution has alreadybeen detected in Di Matteo et al. (2005) and explained by means of a model ofsocial network. Here we show that this model is tested on a broader sample ofcountries having different patterns of social network structure. Thesedifferent social attitudes, measured using a social capital indicator, reflectin the power-law exponent estimates, verifying in this way the existence oflinkages among firms' productivity performance and social network.
label: human

text: This study investigates the relationship between social networks and labor productivity across European countries using a comprehensive empirical framework. Drawing on data from multiple national labor markets, we analyze how informal social connections influence individual and firm-level productivity outcomes. Our findings suggest that stronger social networks facilitate better information flow, knowledge sharing, and trust, which in turn enhance workplace efficiency and innovation. The analysis accounts for industry heterogeneity and institutional differences, revealing that the positive effects of social networks on productivity are more pronounced in knowledge-intensive sectors. Additionally, we explore the role of social capital as a complementary asset to physical and human capital in driving economic performance. The results contribute to the broader understanding of social factors in labor economics and offer policy implications for fostering productive social environments in the European context.
label: llm

text: The space-time geometry is considered to be a physical geometry, i.e. ageometry described completely by the world function. All geometrical conceptsand geometric objects are taken from the proper Euclidean geometry. They areexpressed via the Euclidean world function \sigma_E and declared to be conceptsand objects of any physical geometry, provided the Euclidean world function\sigma_E is replaced by the world function \sigma of the physical geometry inquestion. The set of physical geometries is more powerful, than the set ofRiemannian geometries, and one needs to choose a true space-time geometry. Ingeneral, the physical geometry is multivariant (there are many vectors whichare equivalent to a given vector, but are not equivalent between themselves).The multivariance admits one to describe quantum effects as geometric effectsand to consider existence of elementary particles as a geometrical problem,when the possibility of the physical existence of an elementary geometricobject in the form of a physical body is determined by the space-time geometry.Multivariance admits one to describe discrete and continuous geometries, usingthe same technique. A use of physical geometry admits one to realize thegeometrical approach to the quantum theory and to the theory of elementaryparticles.
label: human

text: This article explores the deformation principle as a foundational approach to the further geometrization of physics, aiming to extend conventional geometric frameworks underlying physical theories. By systematically applying deformation techniques to classical geometric structures, we investigate how physical laws can be reformulated within more generalized, flexible geometric settings. This approach enables a deeper understanding of the interplay between geometry and physical phenomena, revealing novel insights into spacetime structure and field interactions. The proposed framework accommodates both classical and quantum regimes, suggesting a unifying geometric scheme that bridges different scales and forces. We present mathematical formulations and illustrative examples demonstrating how deformed geometries can capture complex physical behaviors traditionally challenging to describe. Our findings also indicate potential pathways for integrating gravity with other fundamental interactions through geometric deformation. The study ultimately contributes to the ongoing quest for a coherent and comprehensive geometric foundation for modern physics.
label: llm

text: We examine gauge theories defined in higher dimensions where theextradimensions form a fuzzy (finite matrix) manifold. First we reinterpret thesegauge theories as four-dimensional theories with Kaluza-Klein modes and then weperform a generalized \`a la Forgacs-Manton dimensional reduction. We emphasizesome striking features emerging in the later case such as (i) the appearance ofnon-abelian gauge theories in four dimensions starting from an abelian gaugetheory in higher dimensions, (ii) the fact that the spontaneous symmetrybreaking of the theory takes place entirely in the extra dimensions and (iii)the renormalizability of the theory both in higher as well as in fourdimensions. Then reversing the above approach we present a renormalizable fourdimensional SU(N) gauge theory with a suitable multiplet of scalar fields,which via spontaneous symmetry breaking dynamically develops extra dimensionsin the form of a fuzzy sphere. We explicitly find the tower of massiveKaluza-Klein modes consistent with an interpretation as gauge theory on $M^4\times S^2$, the scalars being interpreted as gauge fields on $S^2$. Dependingon the parameters of the model the low-energy gauge group can be of the form$SU(n_1) \times SU(n_2) \times U(1)$.
label: human

text: This article explores the concept of fuzzy extra dimensions within the framework of higher-dimensional field theories. We examine the process of dimensional reduction using fuzzy spaces, highlighting how this approach leads to effective lower-dimensional models with noncommutative geometrical features. The dynamical generation of fuzzy extra dimensions is studied, demonstrating mechanisms by which such structures can emerge naturally from the underlying field dynamics. Particular attention is given to the renormalizability of the resulting theories, addressing challenges posed by the non-locality inherent in fuzzy geometries. Through detailed analysis, we show that fuzzy extra dimensions provide a consistent and predictive setting for constructing renormalizable higher-dimensional models. These findings open new avenues for exploring physics beyond the Standard Model by incorporating noncommutative internal spaces.
label: llm

text: We compute the stationary in-degree probability, $P_{in}(k)$, for a growingnetwork model with directed edges and arbitrary out-degree probability. Inparticular, under preferential linking, we find that if the nodes have a lighttail (finite variance) out-degree distribution, then the correspondingin-degree one behaves as $k^{-3}$. Moreover, for an out-degree distributionwith a scale invariant tail, $P_{out}(k)\sim k^{-\alpha}$, the correspondingin-degree distribution has exactly the same asymptotic behavior only if$2<\alpha<3$ (infinite variance). Similar results are obtained whenattractiveness is included. We also present some results on descriptivestatistics measures %descriptive statistics such as the correlation between thenumber of in-going links, $D_{in}$, and outgoing links, $D_{out}$, and theconditional expectation of $D_{in}$ given $D_{out}$, and we calculate thesemeasures for the WWW network. Finally, we present an application to thescientific publications network. The results presented here can explain thetail behavior of in/out-degree distribution observed in many real networks.
label: human

text: This article investigates the asymptotic behavior of in-degree distributions in growing network models where the out-degree distribution is arbitrary but fixed. We consider a broad class of stochastic processes generating directed networks through preferential attachment mechanisms with general out-degree constraints. By analyzing the interplay between the specified out-degree distributions and the resulting in-degree growth, we establish conditions under which the in-degree distribution converges to a limiting form. Our approach utilizes generating functions and branching process approximations to rigorously characterize the tail behavior of the in-degree distribution. The results demonstrate that the limiting in-degree distribution exhibits heavy-tailed properties influenced by both the shape of the out-degree distribution and attachment rules. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical findings and illustrate the range of possible asymptotic behaviors in practical settings. These insights deepen the understanding of structural properties in complex growing networks with heterogeneous link formation patterns.
label: llm

text: The process of self-compensation in Cd0.95Zn0.05Te:Cl solid-solution crystalshas been studied by annealing single crystals under a controlled Cd vaporpressure, with subsequent measurements of the Hall effect, photoluminescence,carrier lifetime and mobility, and photocurrent memory in the annealedcrystals. By means of this annealing, conditions of thermal treatment that makeit possible to fabricate low-conductivity samples with a low carrier density,10E7-10E11 cm-3, are denned. In these samples, a p -- n conduction inversion isobserved at a higher free-carrier density ((n, p) near 10E9 cm-3) and thedependence of the electron density on the Cd vapor pressure exhibits a moregentle slope than in the case of CdTe:Cl crystals.  The obtained data are dis-cussed in terms of a self-compensation model inwhich intrinsic point defects act as acceptors with deep levels. This level isattributed to a Zn vacancy, which remains active at high Cd pressure.
label: human

text: This study investigates the self-compensation mechanisms in Cd0.95Zn0.05Te:Cl crystals subjected to varying cadmium vapor pressures during growth. By systematically altering the Cd vapor pressure, we examine its influence on the electrical conduction properties and defect structure of the doped crystals. Experimental results demonstrate a strong correlation between Cd vapor pressure and the balance of donor and acceptor defects, leading to compensation effects that significantly affect conductivity. The findings provide insight into optimizing crystal growth conditions to control carrier concentration and improve material performance for radiation detectors. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of defect chemistry and electrical compensation in CdZnTe-based semiconductor materials.
label: llm

text: The energy density of the universe today may be dominated by the vacuumenergy of a slowly rolling scalar field. Making a quantum expansion around sucha time dependent solution is found to break fundamental symmetries of quantumfield theory. We call this mechanism cosmological symmetry breaking and arguethat it is different from the standard phenomenon of spontaneous symmetrybreaking. We illustrate this with a toy scalar field theory, whose actiondisplays a U(1) symmetry.
